records.title: Family Medicine Forum Research Proceedings 2014/Compte rendu sur la recherche au Forum en médecine familiale 2014 Compte rendu sur la recherche au Forum en médecine familiale 2014
records.abstract:
Contexte

Le projet de loi 52 soumis à l’Assemblée nationale du Québec propose de légaliser l’aide médicale à mourir. Aucune étude n’a évalué quels gestes cliniques concrets sont interprétés comme de l’aide médicale à mourir par les professionnels de la santé.

Objectif

Explorer la compréhension au plan clinique de l’aide médicale à mourir par les professionnels de la santé.

Type d’étude

Questionnaire auto-administré.

Participants

Médecins et infirmières recrutés lors d’activités de formation continue.

Mesure

Six scénarios cliniques ont décrit différents gestes cliniques posés par un professionnel à une personne en fin de vie, incluant le refus de traitement, l’utilisation d’opiacés ajustés au soulagement des symptômes et la prescription ou l’injection d’un médicament mortel avec ou sans la demande du patient. Le répondant devait statuer s’il considère chacun de ces gestes comme étant ou non une aide médicale à mourir.

Résultats

Des 308 questionnaires distribués, 271 ont été complétés (taux de réponse de 88 %). Sur les 271 participants, 200 sont des infirmières et 71 des médecins. Le pourcentage de répondants qui croient que le scénario correspond à de l’aide médicale à mourir va comme suit : 1) refus de traitement, 64 %; 2) utilisation d’opiacés ajustés au soulagement des symptômes, 39 %; 3) utilisation d’opiacés au-delà de ce qui est nécessaire pour le soulagement des symptômes, 79 %; 4) prescription d’un barbiturique oral administré par le patient, 69 %; 5) injection d’un bloqueur neuromusculaire et d’un barbiturique à la demande du patient, 76 %; 6) injection d’un bloqueur neuromusculaire et d’un barbiturique à la demande d’un proche pour un patient inapte, 74 %.

Conclusion

Il existe une grande variation dans l’interprétation de ce qu’est l’aide médicale à mourir. Une majorité de professionnels croient que des gestes déjà légaux (refus de traitement) et des gestes n’étant pas visés par le projet de loi 52 (injection d’un médicament mortel à une personne inapte) constituent de l’aide médicale à mourir. Il est nécessaire de clarifier quels gestes cliniques concrets sont visés par les propositions de changements législatifs.

Context

Interprofessional learning across the health and social professions is enhanced when based on clinical models. Persons with developmental disabilities offer one such model when trained as simulated patients. This presentation assesses the model’s effectiveness. For 2 consecutive years, members of the Faculty of Medicine and the Faculty of Health Professions at Dalhousie University have presented an interprofessional, elective mini-course for first- and second-year students.

Objective

To name and apply strategies for communicating with persons with developmental disabilities in order to understand their health priorities; to examine the decision-making and consent process for persons with developmental disabilities; and to state the importance of interprofessional communication and person-directed care with persons with developmental disabilities.

Methods

Thirty-six first-year and 46 second-year students completed 3, 1.5-hour sessions in plenary and small group formats. Students from physiotherapy, medicine, occupational therapy, nursing, social work, recreation and leisure, nursing, optometry associate, and audiology took part. Faculty came from the schools of Human Communication Disorder, Occupational Therapy, Social Work, Physiotherapy, Health and Human Performance, and the departments of Family Medicine and Pediatrics. Students’ evaluation of the first-year course involved 11 statements for rating on a 4-point scale (“strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”) and open-ended invitations to suggest improvements and generally comment.

Results

An example feedback statement provided by a participant is as follows: “The expectations of students were clear; the level of difficulty of the information was about right; as the result of this IPHE [interprofessional health education] session, I feel more confident in my capacity to collaborate with other professions.” The participants’ responses informed modifications in the second year of the program. Feedback from the simulated patients and family members indicated a preference for using as much of their own personal history as possible, satisfaction in contributing to teaching of health profession students, and enjoyment in acting assigned roles.

Conclusion

This presentation summarizes the course’s development and the experiences surrounding its implementation. Participants considering interprofessional teaching can expect to be able to identify strengths and challenges of interprofessional curriculum development, the value of employing persons with developmental disabilities as simulated patients and the advantages of using their issues as a focus in applying interprofessional learning, and the administrative and planning challenges in delivering an interprofessional program.

Contexte

Des données ont montré une variabilité dans la pratique des avortements chirurgicaux aux États-Unis. Au Québec et au Canada, aucune donnée n’a été rapportée sur ce sujet.

Objectif

Questionner les professionnels d’un échantillon représentatif de cliniques d’avortement au Canada, pour mieux comprendre leur pratique de l’avortement chirurgical.

Méthodes

Sondage transversal d’envergure nationale.

Participants

Utilisation de sources publiques et de réseaux professionnels pour identifier les cliniques d’avortement partout au Canada.

Instrument de collecte

Adaptation au contexte canadien d’un questionnaire préalablement publié. Envoi de versions anglophone et francophone du questionnaire par voies postale et électronique, de juillet à novembre 2013, en utilisant la technique de Dillman.

Mesures

Lieu des cliniques, techniques d’avortement, caractéristiques des professionnels.

Résultats

Parmi 94 cliniques d’avortement répertoriées au Canada, 78 (83 %) ont participé au sondage. Comme rapportée par les responsables des cliniques, l’information pré-avortement au Québec est donnée par des infirmières autorisées (82,5 %) ou des conseillères agréées/travailleuses sociales (15 %). Dans le reste du Canada, cette tâche incombe aux infirmières autorisées (32,4 %), conseillères agréées/travailleuses sociales (25,5 %) ou médecins (23,5 %). Ce sont les infirmières (77,5 %) et les médecins (12,5 %) qui obtiennent le consentement de la femme au Québec, tandis que dans le reste du Canada, ce sont surtout les médecins (52,9 %) et les conseillères agréées/ travailleuses sociales (26,5 %) qui le font. L’échographie pré-avortement est faite dans 95 % et 97 % des cas, au Québec et dans le reste du Canada, respectivement. Au Québec, ce sont les médecins (61,1 %) et les infirmières (22,2 %) qui font ces échographies, tandis que dans le reste du Canada, ce sont les médecins (43,3 %) et des techniciens agréés (33,3 %). La plupart des avortements chirurgicaux sont obtenus sous bloc cervical avec sédationanalgésie consciente (1er trimestre : 77,8 %; 2e trimestre : 84,4 %) sans différence régionale.

Conclusion

Des variations existent au Canada sur la façon dont les avortements chirurgicaux sont pratiqués, probablement en lien avec la formation et la disponibilité des professionnels de la santé. La connaissance de ces variations a des implications sur l’élargissement de l’accessibilité des services d’avortement au Canada.

Context

There has been limited research using health administrative data to explore how primary care providers and specialists share care for patients with chronic disease. As HIV is a complex condition managed primarily in the outpatient setting, it is a useful condition on which to build a typology of this interface.

Objective

To characterize patterns of care for people living with HIV in Ontario and to use the observed patterns to develop a unique typology of current HIV care in Ontario.

Design

This retrospective, population-based observational study was conducted for the period April 1, 2009, to March 31, 2012.

Population

A validated case ascertainment algorithm was used to identify people with HIV receiving care in Ontario, the Canadian province with the highest prevalence of HIV.

Methods

We derived a typology of care based on previous frameworks by linking patients to usual sources of primary care and to HIV specialists. We identified 5 possible patterns of care, described as disorganized care, exclusively primary care, family physician–dominated comanagement, specialist-dominated comanagement, and exclusively specialist care.

Main outcome measures

Patient and physician characteristics and outpatient visits by care pattern.

Results

The prevalence of each care pattern among the 13 480 eligible individuals was as follows: disorganized care, 1149 (8.6%); exclusively primary care, 6094 (52.7%); family physician–dominated comanagement, 1349 (10.0%); specialist-dominated comanagement, 4118 (30.5%); and exclusively specialist care, 707 (5.2%). Patient characteristics varied among the patterns, with those in specialist-dominated patterns more likely to be younger, female, lower income, residing rurally, from an immigrant population, and with lower ascertained comorbidity. In addition, the characteristics of family physicians varied among the patterns. Patients in both comanagement patterns had, on average, approximately twice as many visits as patients in their respective single-physician models, as well as different patterns of HIV billing.

Conclusion

We anticipate this typology can be applied to other chronic conditions and can be used for assessing the effect of different patterns of care on the quality of care and health of individuals with complex conditions.

Context

The 2012 Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care (CTFPHC) recommendations on screening for type 2 diabetes differ from those proposed by other organizations.

Objective

To determine the use of the CTFPHC clinical practice guideline (CPG) on screening for type 2 diabetes by family physicians.

Design

Cross-sectional descriptive study.

Participants

Family physicians from all 4 family medicine teaching units and 12 family medicine clinics in Quebec city, Que.

Instrument

Questionnaire assessing 1) the use of the CPG according to the awareness-to-adherence model and 2) intention to use it, the determinants of this intention, and the barriers to its use according to the physician guideline compliance model.

Results

Among the 282 eligible physicians, 131 (47%) responded to the questionnaire. Overall, 74% (95% CI 66% to 81%) of respondents knew of the existence of the CTFPHC, 48% (95% CI 40% to 57%) knew of the existence of the CPG, 25% (95% CI 18% to 33%) knew its recommendations, 12% (95% CI 8% to 19%) agreed with it, 10% (95% CI 6% to 17%) adopted it, and 0% adhered to it. These proportions were lower among physicians in medical clinics, with more than half not even knowing of the existence of the CTFPHC. The current practice described by physicians who claimed to follow either the Canadian Diabetes Association or the CTFPHC recommendations did not match those recommendations (57% and 66%, respectively). Contrary to the CTFPHC recommendations, the majority of respondents would prescribe a blood glucose test to an individual with a low risk (76%) or a moderate (94%) risk of diabetes. The intention to implement the CTFPHC recommendations was moderate (mean [SD] score of 4.6 [1.6] out of 7). It was significantly associated with past behaviour related to CPGs, and attitude, socioprofessional norm, and perceived behavioural control vis-à-vis the CPG. The main barriers identified were calculation of the risk for each patient, patients’ expectations, difference between the CTFPHC recommendations and those of other organizations, and lack of time.

Conclusion

The CTFPHC CPG on screening for type 2 diabetes is little known and little used by physicians participating in this study. Strategies to overcome the barriers identified could improve the implementation of this evidence-based CPG and possibly of other CPGs from the CTFPHC.

Contexte

Plusieurs médicaments sont à utiliser avec prudence chez les patients âgés afin de prévenir des effets néfastes. Les critères de Beer fournissent une liste de médicaments potentiellement inappropriés chez les personnes âgées.

Objectifs

Déterminer le pourcentage des patients de 65 ans et plus suivis à l’Unité de médecine familiale du Nord de Lanaudière (UMFNL) ayant une prescription d’un médicament de la liste des critères de Beer. Déterminer s’il y a une justification au dossier des patients pour expliquer les prescriptions de ces médicaments.

Plan

Il s’agit d’une étude rétrospective de qualité de l’acte utilisant des critères explicites.

Participants

Cent cinquante dossiers de patients âgés de 65 ans et plus ont été sélectionnés au hasard parmi les patients suivis par un médecin de famille de l’UMFNL et ayant consulté en visite de suivi entre le 1er juillet 2012 et le 30 juin 2013.

Intervention

Après vérification des critères inclusion/exclusion, les dossiers sélectionnés ont été examinés par deux résidents en médecine familiale dans une approche par « consensus » à l’aide d’une grille de collecte de données.

Résultats

Cent trente-sept dossiers ont été retenus et analysés. Au total, 39 patients (28,5%) avaient une ordonnance pour au moins 1 des 17 médicaments recherchés. Seulement 3 de ces patients avaient une justification documentée au dossier. Les benzodiazépines représentent la majorité des PIM (57,1%), suivie du zopiclone (6,1%), des neuroleptiques (6,1%), de la glyburide (6,1%) et des relaxants musculaires (6,1%).

Conclusion

Malgré les limitations d’une petite étude rétrospective de dossiers, le taux de prescription d’une PIM chez les patients âgés de 65 ans et plus (28,5%) mesuré à l’UMFNL se compare à celui décrit dans une étude similaire à la nôtre conduite à Taiwan en 2009 (19,1%). Les benzodiazépines sont clairement les PIM les plus souvent rencontrées. Le faible taux de documentation au dossier des justifications de l’utilisation d’une PIM mérite d’être soulevé. Parmi les mesures pouvant aider à limiter l’utilisation de PIM chez les personnes âgées, nous croyons qu’une plus vaste étude regroupant les douze UMF de l’Université Laval aiderait à mieux comprendre les caractéristiques des patients susceptibles de recevoir des PIM ainsi que les caractéristiques des prescripteurs.

records.abstract: B.1 Nutrient Regulation of Transcription & Signaling by O-GlcNAc: Fundamental Roles in Diabetes, Neurodegeneration and Cancer Gerald Hart Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, USA O-GlcNAc cycles on and off thousands of nucleocytoplasmic proteins and has extensive crosstalk with protein phosphorylation, both at the site level and by reciprocal regulation of their respective enzymes. O-GlcNAc cycles on nearly all proteins involved in transcription, where it regulates gene expression in response to nutrients. O-GlcNAc also regulates the cycling of the TATA-binding (TBP) protein on and off DNA during the transcription cycle and is required for TBP to bend DNA. Targeted, inducible, deletion of the O-GlcNAc Transferase in αCAMKII positive (excitatory) neurons of adult mice results in a morbidly obese mouse with a satiety defect. Thus, O-GlcNAcylation not only serves as a nutrient sensor in all cells, but also is directly involved in appetite regulation. O-GlcNAcylation also plays an important role in the trafficking of the AMPA receptors in neurons and in the development of functional synaptic spines. Recent studies have shown that more than one-half of all human protein kinases are modified by O-GlcNAc and all kinases that have been tested are indeed regulated in some way by the sugar. Abnormal O-GlcNAcylation of CAMKII contributes directly to diabetic cardiomyopathy and to arrhythmias associated with diabetes. Prolonged elevation of O-GlcNAc, as occurs in diabetes, contributes directly to diabetic complications and is a major mechanism of glucose toxicity. Drugs that elevate O-GlcNAcylation in the brain, which prevents hyperphosphorylation, appear to be of benefit for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease in animal models. To date, all cancers have elevated O-GlcNAc cycling, which may play a key role in the regulation of metabolism in cancer cells. Improvements in HCD/ETD methods have greatly facilitated the study of O-GlcNAcylation. However, mapping sites and measuring stoichiometry of O-GlcNAcylation still remains a formidable challenge to mass spectrometry. Supported by NIH P01HL107153, R01GM116891, R01DK61671, and N01-HV-00240. Dr. Hart receives a share of royalty received by the university on sales of the CTD 110.6 antibody, which are managed by JHU. B.2 Characterization of Glycoproteins by Top Down UVPD Analysis Catherine Going1, Romain Huguet2, Daniel Lopez Ferrer2, Vlad Zabrouskov2, Andreas F. R. Huhmer2, Sharon Pitteri1 1Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, USA; 2Thermo Fisher Scientific, South San Francisco, CA, USA Ultraviolet photodissociation (UVPD) is a powerful tool for top-down proteomics due to the high efficiency and indiscriminant nature of its fragmentation. While UVPD has been demonstrated for glycopeptide and glycan analysis, it has not yet been tested on intact glycoproteins. Mass spectrometry analysis of glycoproteins typically consists of either protein digestion followed by glycopeptide separation and identification by LC-MS/MS, or removal of the glycans and separate LC-MS/MS analysis of the glycans and/or peptides. Key disadvantages of these methods are that glycopeptides can go undetected due to poor ionization efficiency, and that removal of glycans from glycopeptides before mass spectrometry eliminates glycosylation site information. Here we demonstrate the utility of top-down UVPD for analyzing both the composition and locations of glycosylation. Disulfide intact and reduced and alkylated glycoprotein ions were produced by nanoelectrospray ionization. Ions were analyzed on a Thermo Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid MS, and top-down fragmentation was performed on isolated precursors with ultraviolet photodissociation at 213 nm using a solid-state Nd/YAG. UVPD fragmentation of intact glycoproteins produced predominantly a and x ions and preferential fragmentation at proline residues, consistent with previous observations for glycopeptides. UVPD of disulfide reduced ribonuclease B resulted in single amino acid resolution for the site of the glycan, and fragment ions were composed predominantly of cleavage along the protein backbone with retention of the entire glycan, whereas UVPD of disulfide intact ribonuclease B resulted in predominantly cleavage of the entire glycan from the precursor and charge reduced precursor ions, and close to 100% sequence coverage for the termini of the proteins up until the locations of the disulfide bonds. This data demonstrates that complementary information can be gained from top-down UVPD of folded and unfolded glycoproteins – the exact masses of the glycans from UVPD of the folded form of the protein, and the residues on which those glycans are located from UVPD of the unfolded form of the protein. With top-down UVPD of CTLA4, two different glycoforms of the protein with the same mass and same two glycans were identified, demonstrating the unique capability of the top-down method to differentiate glycoforms. B.3 Proteomics as a Tool for Biological Forensics Eric Merkley1, Sarah C. Jenson1, David S. Wunschel2, Karen L. Wahl2, Natalie Heller3, Kristin H. Jarman3 1Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL): 2Chemical and Biological Signature Sciences Group, and 3Statistical Modeling and Experimental Design Group, Richland WA, USA Mass spectrometry-based proteomics is poised to have a significant impact in forensic science and its unique characteristics make it a natural fit for biological forensics. Proteomics, like whole genome sequencing, is one of the few techniques that provide high molecular specificity for a broad range of targets in a single measurement. In addition, the discipline of proteomics is accustomed to careful consideration of error rates, a key requirement for the admissibility of scientific evidence in the courts according to the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals. Recent developments in the field of proteomics, such as increased availability of high-resolution instrumentation, the maturation of computational and statistical methods for estimating and controlling error rates, and the explosive growth of genomic sequence data, have combined to make proteomics a mature discipline that is ready to make an impact in forensics. Many forensic proteomics applications have been described, including microbial characterization and identification, individual identification using hair samples, biofluid identification/serology, and the detection of protein toxins. As with proteomics research in the fundamental life sciences, these studies used a diversity of experimental and data analysis approaches. The proteomics community as a whole has adopted data quality standards and best practices. Forensic proteomics will need similar standards, which must harmonize the best practices of proteomics in basic science with the unique demands of forensic techniques. This presentation discusses the creation of such standards, focusing on two key areas where proteomics methods and forensics practices can find common ground: peptide identification and the use of authentic standards, and selection/construction of a search database. To illustrate these concepts, we will draw from our experience developing a shotgun proteomics method for detection of the protein toxin ricin. B.4 Spectral Library of Mouse Brain Proteome Shenheng Guan, Noah Johnson, Julie Chen, A. L. Burlingame University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA Publicly available 5.2 million high-resolution HCD spectra of mouse brain samples [1] have been processed to generate annotated spectral library of 224 thousands of peptide ions representing 11,004 proteins, with a false discovery rate of 0.03%. The purposes for establishing the high quality mouse brain spectral library are (1) for fast assessing quality of data from mouse brain samples by spectral library search and (2) for selection of peptide ions for quantification using SRM, PRM, or SWATH methods. In-house spectral library generation pipeline includes raw data access, wrapper for MSGF plus database search engine, spectral annotation tool to producing MSP library, and MSP spectral viewer. The MSP spectral library can be converted to other spectral library search engine formats, using one of several conversion tools. Speed of search with NIST MS Search on a desktop PC is about 300spectra/second. To control false discovery rate of spectral library search, distribution of raw dot-product between the query and library spectra is directly used to model positive and negative matches. Several methods for parametric extraction of the score distributions are investigated. Supported by NIH grant 8P41GM103481 and Sheldon G. Adelson Medical Research Foundation. [1] Sharma et al, Nature Neuroscience, 18, 1819–1831 (2015). B.5 Specter: linear deconvolution as a new paradigm for targeted analysis of data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry proteomics Ryan Peckner1, Samuel A. Myers1, Jarrett D. Egertson2, Richard S. Johnson2, Steven A. Carr1, Michael J. MacCoss2, Jacob D. Jaffe1 1The Broad Institute of of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA; 2University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA Mass spectrometry with data-independent acquisition (DIA) has emerged as a promising method to greatly improve the comprehensiveness and reproducibility of targeted and discovery proteomics, in theory systematically measuring all peptide precursors within a biological sample. Despite the technical maturity of DIA, the analytical challenges involved in discriminating between peptides with similar sequences in convoluted spectra have limited its applicability in important cases, such as the detection of single-nucleotide polymorphisms and alternative site localizations in phosphoproteomics data. We have developed Specter, an open-source software tool that uses linear algebra to deconvolute DIA mixture spectra directly in terms of a spectral library, circumventing the problems associated with typical fragment correlation-based approaches. We validate the sensitivity of Specter and its performance relative to other methods by means of several complex datasets, and show that Specter is able to successfully analyze cases involving highly similar peptides that are typically challenging for DIA analysis methods. B.6 Targeting RAS Driven Cancers with Antibodies to Upregulated and Functionally Important Cell-Surface Proteins Alexander J. Martinko1, Charles Truillet1, Olivier Julien1, Juan A. Diaz1, Max Horlbeck1, Gordon Whiteley2, Josip Blonder2, Jonathan Weissman1, Sourav Bandyopadhyay1, Michael Evans1, James A. Wells1 1University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA; 2Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research, Frederick, MD, USA While there have been tremendous efforts to target oncogenic RAS signaling from inside the cell, little effort has focused on the cell-surface. Using quantitative surface proteomics, we discovered a signature of proteins critical for metastasis that are upregulated on cells transformed with KRASG12V, and driven by MAPK pathway signaling. We next generated a toolkit of recombinant antibodies to several RAS induced membrane proteins. We show that five of these targets are broadly distributed on cancer cell lines harboring KRAS mutations. In parallel, a cell-surface CRISPRi screen identified integrin and Wnt signaling proteins as critical to RAS transformed cells. We demonstrate that antibodies to CDCP1, a protein identified by both efforts, can be leveraged to deliver cytotoxic and immunotherapeutic payloads to RAS transformed cancer cells and report for RAS signaling status in vivo. This compendium of data and recombinant antibodies provides a rich resource for approaching a new paradigm of attacking RAS from outside the cell. B.7 Defining Kinase Inhibitor Polypharmacology with Multiplexed Inhibitor Bead Proteomics: Abemaciclib Inhibits Glycogen Synthase Kinase 3 Beta to Activate WNT Signaling Emily M. Cousins, Dennis Goldfarb, Feng Yan, Jose Roques, David Darr, Gary L. Johnson, Michael B. Major University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, NC, USA The cellular and organismal phenotypic response to a small molecule kinase inhibitor is defined collectively by its targets and their functions. Kinase inhibitor polypharmacology—the study of all targets for a given drug—promises to improve drug repurposing efforts and better inform the management of drug toxicities. We leveraged a competitive kinase enrichment proteomics approach using live cells and mice to define the polypharmacology landscape for several clinically active kinase inhibitors, including trametinib, BMS-777607, dasatinib, erlotinib, abemaciclib, ribociclib, and palbociclib. MIB/MS competition analyses of the cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors abemaciclib, palbociclib and ribociclib revealed overlapping and unique kinase targets. We show that in contrast to palbociclib and ribociclib, abemaciclib directly inhibits glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β) kinase activity with an IC50 of 8.67 nM. Consequently, abemaciclib activates β-catenin-dependent WNT signaling, as determined by β-catenin transcriptional activation and β-catenin protein stabilization. These data reveal differential kinase target specificities for CDK4/6 inhibitors that may govern clinical efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities in patients treated with these drugs. More broadly, we highlight the use of an unbiased MIB/MS-based chemical proteomics technology in live cells and in mice to identify targets of kinase inhibitors. Acknowledgment: This work was supported by the following: V Foundation grant number T2014-009 to MBM and GLJ, Gabrielle's Angel Foundation (grant number 85) to MBM, and the NIH T32 Postdoctoral Training Grant in Pulmonology (5T32HL007106-39) to EMC. B.8 Large-scale phosphoproteomics reveals Shp2 phosphatase-dependent regulators of Pdgf receptor signaling Tanveer S. Batth1, Moreno Papetti1, Anamarija Pfeiffer1, Chiara Francavilla2, Jesper V. Olsen1 1NNF Center for Protein Research, Copenhagen, Denmark; 2University of Manchester, Manchester, UK Tyrosine phosphorylation (pTyr) regulates numerous cell signaling pathways in health and disease. However, its detection and quantitation remains challenging due to its low cellular abundance. We applied comprehensive phosphoproteomics to unravel differential regulators of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) initiated signaling networks upon activation by Pdgf-ββ, Fgf-2 or Igf-1, respectively, and identified over 40,000 phosphorylation sites. The analysis revealed RTK-specific regulation of hundreds of tyrosine phosphorylation sites on key adaptor and signaling molecules. We found the tyrosine phosphatase Shp2 to be the master regulator of Pdgfr pTyr signaling. Application of a recently-introduced allosteric Shp2 inhibitor revealed global regulation of the Pdgf-dependent tyrosine phosphoproteome, which significantly altered the interaction of Pdgfr with signaling proteins and impaired cell migration but not cell proliferation. We present a list of hundreds of Shp2-dependent targets and putative substrates including Rasa1 and Cortactin with increased tyrosine phosphorylation, and Gab1 and Erk1/2 with decreased tyrosine phosphorylation. Our study demonstrates that large-scale quantitative phosphoproteomics can precisely dissect tightly regulated kinase/phosphatase signaling networks. B.9 Identification of Predictive Biomarkers For Radiation Injury From Circulating Serum And Urine Exosomes Emily Chen1, A. Ribault2, S. Kulkarni3, A. Koller4 1Columbia University Medical Center, New York, NY, USA; 2Institut de Radioprotection et de Sûreté Nucléaire Fontenay-aux-Roses, France; 3Department of Radiation Oncology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, USA; 4Proteomics Shared Resource at the Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center, CUMC, New York, NY, USA Exosomes are cell-derived vesicles that carry a wide range of molecules including genetic material, proteins and lipids as their cargos. We hypothesize that comprehensive characterization of urine and serum exosomes in response to radiation exposure at various radiation doses and times could lead to a panel of biomarkers that could be used as (i) biodosimetry tool to determine radiation injury and (ii) pharmacodynamic parameter for radio-mitigation screening to quantitatively assess the extent of mitigation. In our recent studies, we analyzed circulating exosomes from serum and urine samples collected from a WBI mouse model and serum exosome collected from a group of patients who underwent pelvic radiation therapy and developed various degrees of acute toxicity in response to radiation. Using quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomics technology and statistical analyses with a B-H FDR correction, we detected and quantified 321 proteins from urine exosome and 674 proteins from serum exosome. From the human cohort, we detected and quantified 547 proteins from serum exosome. For the WBI mouse model study, we identified 23 biomarkers from urine and 24 biomarkers from serum exosomes indicative of radiation-induced injury. Urinary exosome signatures identified different physiological parameters than the ones obtained in serum exosomes. Exosome signatures from urine indicated injury to the liver, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. In contrast, serum showed vascular injuries and acute inflammation in response to radiation. For the human cohort study, we identified 71 biomarkers that correlate with 3 grades of radiation-induced toxicity. Furthermore, among biomarkers associated with high grade of radiation-induced toxicity, 6 of these proteins were also found in the radiation injury signature we identified from the WBI mouse model. Together, these data showed the feasibility of defining biomarkers that could elucidate tissue-associated and systemic response caused by ionizing radiation. This is the first report using an exosome proteomics approach to identify signatures of radiation-induced injury. B.10 Quantitative comparison of the O-GlcNAcome in Female and Male Embryonic Stem Cells Jason C. Maynard1, Elizabeth Allene Martin2, Barbara Panning2, A. L. Burlingame1 Departments of 1Pharmaceutical Chemistry, 2Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA DNA methylation occurring at the 5′ position of cytosines is a key epigenetic regulator of mammalian embryogenesis and stem cell differentiation. Levels of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) are determined by DNMT and TET proteins. DNMTs add methyl groups to CpG dinucleotides to generate 5mC, while TET proteins catalyze oxidation of 5mC to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC). 5hmC can lead to demethylation by iterative TET-mediated oxidation and base excision repair. Female mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) have dramatically reduced levels of 5mC relative to male ESCs. This reduction is unique to ESCs, which have two active X chromosomes, unlike somatic cells, since X-inactivation equalizes gene dosage between sexes. These results suggest the two-fold increase in expression of X-linked genes direct hypomethylation in XX ESCs. A candidate for this X-linked gene is Ogt, which encodes O-GlcNAc transferase. Female ESCs produce twice as much OGT as males; and OGT directly interacts with and modifies TET proteins. We sought to determine whether OGT modifies more unique proteins involved in the DNA methylation pathway in female ESCs compared to males. We have enriched for O-GlcNAc modified peptides using lectin weak affinity chromatography and quantitatively assessed the O-GlcNAcome of male and female embryonic stem cells using SILAC based mass spectrometry approaches. We found increased O-GlcNAcylation on TET1 in female ESCs compared to males which may be aiding in the hypomethylation observed in the female cells. Acknowledgements: Mass spectrometry analysis was provided by the UCSF Mass Spectrometry Facility directed by A. L. Burlingame, supported by 8P41GM103481 and the Adelson Medical Research Foundation. B.11 Investigation of novel MELK interacting proteins and signaling pathways in triple-negative breast cancer Ian M. McDonald, Raquel C. Martinez Chacin, Xianxi Wang, Laura E. Herring, Michael J. Emanuele, Lee M. Graves University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, NC, USA In women, breast cancer is the most commonly occurring type of cancer, and the second leading cause of cancer deaths. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) accounts for 12–17% of all breast cancers. Patients with TNBC have markedly lower survival rates than those with other breast cancer subtypes, partially due to a lack of effective targeted therapies. Notably, MELK (Maternal Embryonic Leucine zipper Kinase) has recently been implicated in TNBC, along with other difficult to treat cancers. Increased MELK expression in TNBC is correlated with radioresistance, tumor grade, and poor prognosis. Correspondingly, MELK depletion slows proliferation of both TNBC cells and xenografts, and sensitizes them to radiation. Finally, the compound OTSSP167, developed as a MELK inhibitor, is currently in phase 1/2 clinical trials for solid tumors, TNBC, and leukemia, demonstrating significant therapeutic interest in this kinase. Remarkably, the precise function of MELK in cancer is poorly understood. MELK has been implicated in varied processes, including cell cycle progression, cancer stem cell phenotype, and protein translation. Specifically, evidence suggests that in mitosis MELK phosphorylates and activates FoxM1, an oncogenic transcription factor and master regulator of mitotic genes. However, the phosphorylation site has not been determined and mechanisms underlying increased FoxM1 transcriptional activity following phosphorylation by MELK have not been elucidated. Using mass spectrometry (MS), I have identified Ser481 of FoxM1 as a putative MELK phosphorylation site. In collaboration with the Emanuele Lab, FoxM1-S481D and -S481E phosphomimetic mutants were found to have increased activity using a FoxM1 reporter assay. Experiments to further validate and determine the mechanistic effects of this phosphorylation are ongoing. In addition to the FoxM1 relationship, there is a clear need for further investigation into the function and regulation of MELK to elucidate its importance in cancer. To date, few MELK substrates have been definitively validated. The identification of kinase substrates by co-IP can be difficult due to the transient nature of phosphorylation events. One alternative to this approach is proximity-dependent biotin identification, or BioID. This technique utilizes a promiscuous biotin ligase (BirA*) fused to a protein of interest to irreversibly biotinylate proximal proteins in cells, and ultimately detect them by MS. Preliminary BioID experiments using an N-terminal BirA*-MELK fusion protein identified numerous cell cycle-related putative MELK interactors, including CDK1/cyclin B, the MCM complex (MCM2–7), and p53. Efforts to validate these proteins as bona fide MELK interactors, and to determine the nature of these interactions, are ongoing. Additionally, phosphoproteomics and multiplexed inhibitor beads/mass spectrometry (MIB/MS) will be used as complementary approaches to better understand relevant MELK signaling pathways in TNBC. B.12 Characterizing the inducible degradation of mutant PIK3CA using mass spectrometry Lilian Phu, Kyle A. Edgar, Kyung Song, William Forrest, Lori Friedman, Donald S. Kirkpatrick Genentech, South San Francisco, CA, USA Phosphotidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) is one of the most frequently altered signaling pathways in cancer. Mutations in the PIK3CA gene, which encodes the p110alpha subunit of class IA PI3K enzymes, are transforming and result in increased kinase activity and activation of downstream signaling. We have discovered that the PI3K inhibitor, Taselisib (GDC-0032), a novel, oral, selective inhibitor of p110alpha, sparing inhibition of p110beta, is more potent against cancer cells bearing mutations in the PIK3CA gene than those with wild-type PIK3CA. Taselisib treatment induces more apoptotic cell death in PIK3CA mutant cancer cells in comparison to other PI3K inhibitors. Taselisib has a dual mechanism of action, both blocking PI3K kinase signaling, and resulting in a decrease in p110alpha protein levels. To better understand the effect of Taselisib on p110alpha, an approach to quantify the levels of wild-type versus mutant p110alpha was desired. Quantification of each form via immunoblotting was not possible since cell lines harboring PIK3CA mutations are heterozygous and current antibodies against p110alpha cannot distinguish between wild-type and mutant p110alpha. Therefore, a mass spectrometric approach was applied to quantify levels of each type of p110alpha (WT vs. mutant). MS analysis revealed that Taselisib treatment leads to the specific depletion of mutant p110alpha without significant change in the wild-type protein. B.13 High throughput proteomics approach reveals mechanistic basis of acute viral pathogenesis mediated by an RNAi suppressor protein in insect cells Arabinda Nayak1, Michael J. Trnka1, Kathy Li1, Craig Kerr2, Eric Jan2, A. L. Burlingame1, Raul Andino1 1University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA; 2University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC, Canada Confronted with viral pathogens, insects use RNA interference (RNAi) to defend themselves. Accordingly, viral RNAi suppressors engage insect RNAi immunity and modulate viral pathogenesis. Cricket Paralysis Virus (CrPV) infects a broad range of insects and causes acute infections in both Drosophila and mosquito cells in contrast to the majority of the insect viruses, which cause persistent infections. Hence, CrPV provided an ideal platform to interrogate the molecular components of insect immunity that fight virus infection and dissect viral mechanisms that mediate either acute or persistent infections in insects. We employ affinity purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS) alongside biochemical, genomic, and virology approaches to show that CrPV RNAi suppressor protein CrPV-1A hijacks an E3-ubiquitin ligase machinery to degrade RNAi antiviral protein Ago2. Independent of Ago2 antagonism, CrPV-1A interacts with cellular transcription machinery contributing to acute pathogenesis. In summary, this study provides mechanistic insight of the integrated virulence mechanism employed by an RNAi suppressor protein to induce acute pathogenesis in insect cells and may serve as a paradigm for understanding the fundamental principles of disease pathogenesis in insects and the transmission of viral pathogens to humans and other hosts. Acknowledgments: This work was financially supported by DARPA grant HR0011–11-C-0094 to R.A., NIH grant AI091575 to R.A., NIH grant by 8P41GM103481 to A.L.B. and the Adelson Medical Research Foundation to A.L.B. B.14 Chemoproteomic Approaches Toward Small Molecule Support in Drug Discovery Victoria Pham1, James Crawford2, Kyle Edgar2, Lori Friedman2, Nico Ghilardi3, Adam Johnson4, Arna Katewa3, Wendy Lee4, Steven A. Staben2, Wendy Young2, Jennie R. Lill1 1Department of Protein Chemistry, 2Medicinal Chemistry, 3Immunology, 4Biochemical & Cellular Pharmacology, Genentech Inc., South San Francisco, CA, USA Phenotypic screening has played an important role in drug discovery and development over the past decade. Once the small molecule is determined to cause a phenotypic alteration, follow-up work is necessary to decipher the target(s) of interest. Several complementary techniques have been utilized for this purpose. One such method is the use of chemoproteomics where the probes are generated by derivatizing the small molecule inhibitor with a particular functional group allowing for the isolation of the target(s) of interest. Traditionally, a biotin tag attached to the small molecule of interest via an alkyl chain or other linker is employed where the target(s) can be isolated using either avidin or streptavidin resin. While this method is straightforward and relatively cost effective, there are several caveats: 1) non-specific binding of background proteins to the beads and alkyl chain, 2) identifying low abundant proteins can be challenging, and 3) potential loss of activity or solubility can occur upon derivatization. In order to address these issues, several functional groups have been introduced to alleviate these problems. Here we focused on 2 new chemoproteomic platforms: the HaloTag and Caprotec Capture Compound. Their advantages & limitations will be discussed. Method: The HaloTag1 (Promega, Wisconsin) and Capotec Capture Compound2 (Caprotec, Germany) approaches were compared using a BTK inhibitor in a positive control cell line (Ramos B cells) and a negative control cell line (Jurkat T cells). In addition, PI3K inhibitor was tested in a carcinoma cell line (HCC1954 cells) known to express PI3K. B.30 Antibodies to biotin enable large-scale detection of biotinylation sites on proteins Tanya Svinkina1, Namrata D. Udeshi1, Kayvon Pedram2, Shaunt Fereshetian1, Samuel A. Myers1, Ozan Aygun1, Karsten Krug1, Karl Clauser1, Dominic Ryan3, Tslil Ast1,4, Vamsi K. Mootha1,4, Alice Y. Ting2, Steven A. Carr1 1Proteomics, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA; 2Departments of Genetics, Biology, and Chemistry, Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA; 3DRI2 LLC, Littleton, Massachusetts, USA; 4Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Department of Molecular Biology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA A huge challenge facing the field of proteomics is the critical need to identify the exact sites of protein biotinylation for studies involving nitrosylation, sulfenylation, cross-linking mass spectrometry, cell surface proteomics, and proximity labeling of proteins by BioID or APEX to confidently define their compartmental location and topology. To date, these analyses have leveraged the biotin-streptavidin system, a powerful and widely used tool in biotechnology. The appeal stems from the remarkable strength of the non-covalent interaction between biotin and streptavidin. However, the strength of the biotin-streptavidin interaction becomes a liability because harsh, denaturing conditions are necessary to break these interactions and recovery of biotinylated peptides is generally poor. Alternate methods for eluting biotinylated proteins from streptavidin have long been pursued, but all have fallen short of achieving reproducible, large-scale identification of biotinylation sites. Here we present a simple, easy to implement approach that largely overcomes this significant limitation. In this work, we used antibodies directed against biotin to enrich biotinylated peptides in a similar manner to the use of antibodies to enrich post-translational modifications such as ubiquitinylated (GG stub) peptides, acetylated peptides, etc. We show that anti-biotin antibodies enable detection of thousands of sub-stoichiometric biotinylation sites from cellular lysates. To demonstrate the potential of our new approach, we leverage anti-biotin antibodies to identify biotinylation sites from APEX mediated proximity-labeling samples and show that it is vastly superior to conventional methods. Live-cell proximity-labeling using APEX peroxidase followed by anti-biotin enrichment and mass spectrometry yielded over 1600 biotinylation sites on hundreds of proteins, an increase of more than 30-fold in the number of biotinylation sites identified compared to streptavidin-based enrichment at the protein level. The improved workflow for the enrichment of biotinylation sites can be used in multiple applications, for example, analysis of membrane topology, cell surface labeling sites, mapping sites of sulfenylation, and many others. B.31 Direct in-gel profiling of protease specificity - DIPPS Robert Vidmar, Matej Vizovisek, Dusan Turk, Boris Turk, Marko Fonovic Jozef Stefan Institute, Ljubljana, Solvenia Determination of protease specificity is of crucial importance for understanding protease function and also for the design of selective synthetic peptide substrates. Despite several available proteomic methodologies protease cleavage specificity profiling still remains a labor intensive and experimentally challenging task. To tackle these drawbacks, we developed a first gel-based label-free proteomic approach that enables quick and reliable determination of protease cleavage specificity (Vidmar et al., 2017, EMBO journal). The presented methodology is based on in-gel digestion of the gel-separated proteome with the studied protease, enrichment of cleaved peptides by gel extraction and subsequent mass spectrometry analysis combined with a length-limited unspecific database search. We developed an optimized and easy-to-implement workflow that enables the identification of both N- and C-terminal cleavage sequences, which are aligned to establish a global protease cleavage specificity profile. The methodology was validated by profiling ten proteases from highly specific caspase-7, legumain, endoproteinase GluC and trypsin to broad specific matrix-metalloproteinase-3, thermolysin and cathepsins K, L, S and V. Specificity profiling of thermolysin was performed at its optimal temperature of 75eC, which confirmed the applicability of DIPPS to extreme experimental conditions. Furthermore, DIPPS enabled us to perform a first global cleavage specificity profile of legumain at a pH as low as 4.0, which confirmed a pH-dependent cleavage specificity switch. The obtained data of >50 000 cleavages showed excellent correlation with known protease specificities, demonstrating the applicability of this approach to all major mechanistic classes of proteases under a broad range of experimental conditions. This approach can be easily implemented by any proteomic laboratory and thus provides an excellent starting point for protease characterization and development of specific protease substrates and inhibitors. B.32 Identification of the Hedgehog Signalling Modulator Dynarrestin Susanne Höing1,2, Ting-Yu Yeh3, Matthias Baumann2, Nancy Martinez4, Lea Kremer4, Hannes C. A. Drexler1, Philipp Kuchler4, Slava Ziegler4, Peter Reinhardt1,5, Peter Habenberger2, Axel Choidas2, Mia Zischinsky2, Gunther Zischinsky2, Lydia Wagner1,5, R. Masin Abo-Rady1,5, Peter Nussbaumer2, Bert Klebl2, Trina Schroer3, Hans R. Schöler1,6, Herbert Waldmann4, Jared L. Sterneckert1,5 1Max Planck Institute for Molecular Biomedicine, Munster, Germany; 2Lead Discovery Center GmbH, Dortmund, Germany; 3Department of Biology, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA;4Department of Chemical Biology, Max Planck Institute for Molecular Physiology, Dortmund, Germany; 5DFG-Research Center for Regenerative Therapies Dresden, Cluster of Excellence / Technische Universität Dresden, Dresden, Germany; 6University of Münster, Medical Faculty, Münster, Germany Aberrant hedgehog (Hh) signaling contributes to the pathogenesis of multiple cancers. Currently available inhibitors target Smoothened, which can acquire mutations causing drug resistance. A major challenge is to identify compounds that inhibit Hh signaling downstream of Smoothened. We identified dynarrestin, a novel aminothiazole that inhibited Hh signaling and the proliferation of Hh-dependent tumor cells. Chemicalproteomics isolated dynein as the target of dynarrestin. Dyneins convert energy from ATP hydrolysis into motor activity and are essential for many cellular processes, including Hh signaling. We demonstrate that dynarrestin inhibits multiple dynein-dependent processes including endosomal trafficking, mitotic spindle assembly, microtubule sliding, and Smoothened trafficking without disrupting dyneindependentATP hydrolysis. In addition, dynarrestin does not disturb ciliogenesis, which could induce ciliopathy pathogenesis in vivo. Therefore, dynarrestin will be a valuable tool for studying dynein-dependent cellular processes and may form the basis of medicinal chemistry programs for anticancer drugs targeting Hh signaling downstream of Smoothened. B.33 Comprehensive proteome characterization and improved strategies for multi-PTM analysis Juan A. Oses-Prieto1, Jason Maynard1, Shreya Chand1,2, A. L. Burlingame1 1University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA; 2Alkahest, San Carlos, CA, USA Biological systems are modulated at the protein level by a variety of different mechanisms, in many cases involving posttranslational modification (PTM) of particular residues on polypeptides; PTMs affect and regulate the activities of the polypeptides in myriad ways – many of which are yet to be defined and are certainly not understood functionally. Due to the inherent sub-stoichiometric nature of PTMs, PTM-containing peptides are grossly under-sampled in proteomic analysis of digests from complex biological mixtures. Detection and identification of these relatively low abundance peptides, present in a matrix of abundant non-modified components, is a challenging task. To address this problem, strategies for selective enrichment of different types of PTM-containing peptides have been developed. The dotation of PTMs is dynamic in nature; simultaneous changes can occur in different PTMs over the same or different sets of proteins involved on the same process or signaling pathway, with stimulatory or inhibitory modifications of different origin (phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitylation,…). Thus, in order to have clear molecular level details of the signaling events, development of optimized multi-stage PTM enrichment strategies is critical for providing a comprehensive view of the cellular state and understanding the complexity of signaling networks in cells. Recently a protocol has been reported based on integrating sequential purification steps for phosphorylated, ubiquitylated and acetylated peptide components from the same sample, followed by MS analysis (Mertins P, et al. Integrated proteomic analysis of post-translational modifications by serial enrichment. Nat Methods. 2013 Jul;10(7):634–637). We are performing experiments to design an optimized protocol to perform sequential enrichments of these and additional enrichment techniques for different PTMs (S/T and Y phosphorylation, O-GlcNAcylation, acetylation, ubiquitylation). We are using tryptic digests obtained from SILAC labelled cellular extracts to assess the effects of the order of different PTM enrichment techniques (TiO2 chromatography for phosphorylation, IP for acetylation, ubiquitination and tyrosine phosphorylation, lectin affinity for O-GlcNAc), and of selective removal competing modified species (PNGaseF pretreatment) on the recovery efficiency of the different modified species. Additional criteria for evaluation of the success of the different protocols include total number of peptides found, and selectivity assessed by percentage of modified species in the fractions collected. The large parameter space that must be explored in order to unite different enrichment methods in a sequential manner is the main challenge in this endeavor. In order to be able to explore such a space of possible configurations, we are exploring binomial combinations and restricting the number of initial configurations to consider by making some reasonable assumptions (i.e., all immunoaffinity based techniques should be done consecutively, since this would minimize buffer substitutions). Successful integration will arise also from minimizing losses of material in the different steps due to extended handling, buffer and solvent changes, minimizing the amount of sample necessary and to ensuring maximal compatibility between the different techniques/strategies used for each particular PTM enrichment. The ultimate result of the development of these integrated techniques will be increasing the dimensional space of the analysis of biomedical problems by achieving maximum depth of analysis for single PTMs and incorporating multiple PTMs into the data matrix. This will facilitate the integration of data into pathways to achieve a systems biology view of the problem, and understanding of the inter-related role of multiple PTMs. This work was supported by the Dr. Miriam and Sheldon G. Adelson Medical Research Foundation and NIH grants P41GM103481 and 1S10OD016229. B.34 Library-Free DIA for PTM Identification and Quantification using PIQED: Application to Multiple Diet-Induced Acylation Changes in Mouse Liver Mitochondrial Proteins Jesse G. Meyer1, Samir Softic2, Natan Basisty1, Guo-Xiao Wang2, Sushanth Mukkamalla1, Hanno Steen3, Alexey I. Nesvizhskii4,5, Eric Verdin1, Bradford W. Gibson1, Christopher B. Newgard6, C. Ronald Kahn2, Birgit Schilling1 1Buck Institute for Research on Aging, Novato, California, USA; 2Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA; 3Department of Pathology at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA; 4Department of Computational Medicine and Bioinformatics, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; 5Department of Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; 6Sarah W. Stedman Nutrition and Metabolism Center, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC, USA Data-independent acquisition (DIA) is an increasingly utilized method for peptide identification and quantification by mass spectrometry. Identification of peptides by DIA requires a spectral library, usually from past or parallel sample analysis using data-dependent acquisition (DDA). However, recent tools have demonstrated that extraction of correlated precursor and fragment ion signals can be used to generate pseudo-MS/MS spectra from DIA data, which can then be used to identify peptides using traditional database search algorithms. As an extension of this method, we recently developed a software tool and workflow which combines multiple open-source tools to enable completely automated Post-translational modification (PTM) Identification and Quantification Exclusively from DIA (PIQED). This approach is especially beneficial when there is no pre-existing spectral library, which is often the case in studies of novel PTMs, and when studies require many replicates or when sample quantity is limiting. In this work, we used PIQED to identify and quantify site-level acetylation and succinylation changes in mouse liver mitochondria proteins induced by six different diets collected after 2 weeks or 10 weeks, for a total of 12 dietary conditions: (1) chow control, (2) chow + fructose, (3) chow + glucose, (4) high-fat diet (HFD), (5) HFD + fructose, or (6) HFD + glucose. In parallel, we measured changes in mitochondrial protein quantities using Spectronaut. We find that many protein-level changes occur in mitochondrial-associated ribosomal proteins, as well as proteins involved in lipid/hormone metabolism. At the modification level, alterations in protein acetylation are more common than protein succinylation. Notably, we find that many diet-induced changes in site-level protein acetylation and succinylation occur on lysine residues that were not previously determined to be regulated by Sirt3 or Sirt5. After 10 weeks, we find that HFD generally results in decreased protein acetylation, and either sugar generally results in protein hyperacetylation. Although many of the site-level modification changes appear to be a concerted bulk response to diet, there are sugar-specific deviations from the overall trend in proteins within electron transport, amino acid metabolism, beta-oxidation, and the citric acid cycle. Together, this unique combination of multiple quantitative, systems-level measurements, i.e. proteins, protein acylation, and metabolites, provides high-definition molecular understanding of how liver mitochondria respond to dietary glucose, fructose, and fat. B.35 Quantitative proteomic characterization of an isogenic model of the 22q11.2 syndrome deletion generated by CRISPR/Cas9 engineering Yu-Hsiu Lin, Neha P. Paranjape, Arun P. Wiita University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA Copy number variation (CNV) in the genome, due to gains or losses of specific DNA regions, can be causative of human disease. However, unlike single gene disorders, CNV-associated syndromes can arise from complex underlying genetic bases that translate to diverse phenotypic outcomes that are not fully understood. Recently, CRISPR/Cas9 has been employed to engineer CNVs up to 2 Mb to study implications of these structural changes (Kraft et al. Cell Rep (2015) 10:833), but it remains unclear if engineering larger CNVs is feasible. As a proof-of-principle, we sought to develop an isogenic model of the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DS), the most common microdeletion disorder in humans. The 22q11.2 locus is highly susceptible to genomic rearrangements due to the presence of low copy repeats (LCR), with 85% of 22q11.2DS patients carrying a single-copy nearly 3-Mb deletion flanked by the two repeat regions LCR22A and LCR22D. Using a recently-described strategy (Tai et al. Nat Neurosci (2016) 19:517), we took advantage of these regions of nearly-identical sequence to design a single guide that targets both LCRs simultaneously to generate the microdeletion via non-homologous end joining on the resulting breakpoints. In initial gene dosage screening by qPCR, we achieved an encouraging success rate of nine out of 44 (20%) isogenic HEK293T clones harboring the deletion. We further validated the designed deletion by SNP microarray. Our initial goals in generating this model were to investigate 1) whether quantitative proteomics could distinguish protein level changes across this deleted region versus WT cells, pointing to a potential role in diagnostic evaluation and 2) whether individual clones harboring the same genetic deletion exhibit variability at the level of protein abundance, either expressed within the deleted locus or elsewhere in the genome, analogous to the variable phenotypic penetrance found in 22q11.2DS patients. We therefore characterized three deletion-positive clones using label-free quantitative proteomics. Our single-shot analysis on a Thermo Q-Exactive Plus over a 3.5 hour LC gradient detected nine of 43 annotated proteins mapped to the CNV region. As expected, we found a significant decrease in the mean expression of proteins encoded in the deletion locus, with moderate clone-to-clone variation, compared to the mean expression of other genes on Chr22 as well as across the genome. To varying degrees, all nine proteins exhibited lower average abundances in the clonal population when compared to the WT, suggesting that label-free quantification can detect these relatively subtle protein-level changes (predicted 33% decrease in HEK293T cells). However, label-free quantitative proteomics could not distinguish statistically significant changes elsewhere in the proteome that may relate to the phenotypic changes in 22q11.2DS. Taken together, we show that the single guide strategy can efficiently generate CNVs up to ∼3 Mb. These approaches can be used for downstream functional and proteomic studies, in more clinically relevant stem cell and murine models, to better dissect the spectrum of effects of syndromic CNVs.
